strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: forecasting later pretraining loss from an early run of the target model. Decomposing loss by token position provides an interpretable empirical perspective and a potentially useful alternative to transferring hyperparameters from smaller models.
The experimental coverage is substantial: LLaMA-style models from 9.8M to 6.7B parameters, additional GPT-NeoX and MoE fitting experiments, and evaluations on Pile, C4, LAMBADA, and WikiText.

The evaluation includes genuine extrapolation to subsequent training checkpoints, beyond fitting complete trajectories. Figures 3 and 5 report consistently lower forecasting MSE than the three tested baselines across model sizes and observation windows.

The data-mixture application provides encouraging practical evidence: the selected mixtures improve final perplexity in all four reported model/distribution settings and benchmark performance in 12 of 14 comparisons. Equations, architecture tables, package versions, and pseudocode also help readers understand the approach.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not isolate the benefit of token-position modeling. The proposed method incorporates a piecewise temporal function and knowledge of the cosine schedule, whereas the aggregate-loss baselines use simpler functions without equivalent schedule information. After freezing a0 and a1, Equation 10 itself reduces to a constant plus a cosine. A baseline fitting the same temporal forms directly to aggregate loss, together with comparison to relevant schedule-aware prediction methods such as the cited Luo et al. (2025), is needed to substantiate the claimed advantage.

The reported functional-form comparisons contain a material inconsistency. Section 2.3 states that power-law fits have R² below 0.75 for over 95% of checkpoints, whereas Table 9 reports R² above 0.95 for 67% of checkpoints in the 58M ID setting. Table 9 also reports strongly negative in-sample R² for exponential forms containing an additive offset, raising questions about fitting constraints or convergence. These results need reconciliation and fitting diagnostics before the comparative evidence is dependable.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful implementation overview. Algorithm 1, lines 29–30, applies calibration when Npred ≤ Nsep, contradicting the condition in Section 2.4. Outlier filtering, fitting initialization and constraints, and checkpoint evaluation frequency are insufficiently specified. The manuscript also provides no implementation or checkpoint-loss release link. These omissions matter because early extrapolation can be sensitive to fitting choices.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence does not establish reliable ranking at the claimed early cutoff. Selection uses 10B of 400B tokens, or 2.5%, while the main forecasting experiments start at 10%. The paper does not report predicted versus observed endpoints for all five candidates, the exact candidate mixtures, or variability across independent runs or candidate pools. The modest perplexity gains are encouraging, but averaging the last five checkpoints does not establish their statistical reliability.

The generality claims exceed the demonstrated forecasting scope. The main experiments share Pile training data, one tokenizer, and cosine decay. The linear-schedule experiment changes the functional form and reports full-trajectory fit quality; the GPT-NeoX and MoE extensions likewise report fitting rather than early forecasting. These results support empirical regularities under the tested recipes, with broader predictive generalization still unresolved.

The theoretical interpretation needs qualification. Appendix C rejects exponential decay after setting its additive asymptote to zero, although an offset exponential can converge to a positive loss. Equation 17 follows from manually freezing a0 and a1, so it is conditional on that modeling assumption. Figure 11 and the three suppression experiments support approximate late-stage uniformity and competitiveness of ordinary averaging, but do not establish that position weighting is generally unnecessary.
